lines.say: These are the ghost stories of La Porte County, Indiana.
And this is the history behind them: what's real, what's legend, and what no one can prove.

lines.say: La Porte is French for “the door.” The name is said to come from a natural opening in the forest, a doorway onto the prairie.

lines.say: For generations before any settlers came, this was Potawatomi land.

Under treaties signed in 1826 and 1832, the Potawatomi ceded their land here to the United States. In 1838, the government forced hundreds of Potawatomi people to leave Indiana for Kansas. The march is remembered as the Trail of Death. Potawatomi people still live in the region today.
lines.tts: Under treaties signed in eighteen twenty-six and eighteen thirty-two, the Potawatomi ceded their land here to the United States. In eighteen thirty-eight, the government forced hundreds of Potawatomi people to leave Indiana for Kansas. The march is remembered as the Trail of Death. Potawatomi people still live in the region today.

lines.say: A place where so much has come and gone leaves stories behind. Some are history. Some are legend. Many are a little of both.
In this film, we'll tell you which is which, as best the records allow.
In 1853, a young music teacher named Harriet Colfax moved from Ogdensburg, New York, to Michigan City, with her brother.

lines.say: Every evening, she lit the lamps. At first they burned lard oil. It had to be heated first, and on cold nights it could harden again before she got it to the light.

In 1871, a second light was built out on the pier, at the end of a long, raised wooden walkway. A few years later, it was moved to the west pier, across Trail Creek. To reach it, she rowed across the creek in a small boat.

lines.say: She kept the light for forty-three years. People called her Old Faithful.

lines.say: She didn't keep it alone. Ann Hartwell, a teacher she had known in Ogdensburg, followed her to Michigan City and lived with her at the lighthouse. The National Park Service calls Ann her lifelong companion.
Ann taught in the public schools for about twenty-five years, then opened a book exchange that became the area's first lending library.

lines.say: John H. Barker ran the Haskell and Barker Car Company, which built thousands of railroad freight cars a year. In 1905, he turned his family's home into a mansion of thirty-eight rooms.

lines.say: Both of Catherine Barker's parents died in 1910. When her father died that December, newspapers across the country reported that his entire fortune, thirty million dollars, went to her. She was fourteen.
lines.tts: Both of Catherine Barker's parents died in nineteen ten. When her father died that December, newspapers across the country reported that his entire fortune, thirty million dollars, went to her. She was fourteen.

lines.say: Victorians lived close to death, and they had rules for it. Clocks were stopped at the hour of a death. Mirrors were covered. Families wore black, sometimes for years, and had photographs taken of the dead.
The mansion's October candlelight tours are about those Victorian superstitions. But the museum is clear about what they are not.
This is not a haunted house, paranormal investigation, or ghost tour.

lines.say: Fifty years earlier, though, some people in La Porte believed they could do more than mourn the dead. They believed they could talk with them.
In the spring of 1848, two young sisters in Hydesville, New York, said they could talk with a spirit through rapping sounds. Within a few years, Spiritualism had spread across the country.
lines.tts: In the spring of eighteen forty-eight, two young sisters in Hydesville, New York, said they could talk with a spirit through rapping sounds. Within a few years, Spiritualism had spread across the country.
lines.lower: The Fox sisters | 1852

lines.say: Believers sat in circles in darkened rooms, hands on a table, and waited for the dead to answer.

lines.say: Charles W. Cathcart was one of La Porte County's leading men. Born on the island of Madeira in 1809, he went to sea as a boy, settled near La Porte in 1831, and served in the Indiana Senate, in Congress, and, briefly, in the United States Senate.
lines.tts: Charles W. Cathcart was one of La Porte County's leading men. Born on the island of Madeira in eighteen oh nine, he went to sea as a boy, settled near La Porte in eighteen thirty-one, and served in the Indiana Senate, in Congress, and, briefly, in the United States Senate.

v.head: CHARLES W. CATHCART
rows: Born on Madeira, 1809. At sea as a boy.

lines.say: He was a skeptic. When a family named Poston began holding spirit circles nearby, on a farm along the stage road between La Porte and Westville, he went to expose them.
lines.lower: A seance in New York | 1909

lines.say: He built a gadget of his own: a paper tube of phosphorus, sulfur and acid that, turned upside down, would light up a dark room in a flash. He called it his lightning bug.
lines.lower: Emma Hardinge, Modern American Spiritualism | 1870

lines.say: The lights went out, and the music began. A spirit the circle called Old King took up a bass drum, fastened to a frame above the table.
Cathcart slipped his lightning bug onto the middle of the table.

In the Spiritual Telegraph, a Spiritualist newspaper in New York, he described what everyone saw: the stick beating the drum, as if handled from above, with no mortal nearer than about eight feet of it.
lines.lower: Cathcart's account, reprinted in Modern American Spiritualism | 1870

lines.say: What a picture for an artist, he wrote. Then, he said, the stick rose, drew a slow curve in the air, and dropped gently onto the shoulder of the Postons' daughter, the circle's medium.
The skeptic was won over. Soon his own family was holding circles at home, with music, moving furniture and voices. His youngest child, he wrote, could see the spirits.
lines.lower: A seance in New York | 1909

lines.say: He even made a joke of it. With many I have lost my standing as a philosopher, he wrote, but with all, I have won the reputation of a first-rate lamplighter.
By 1858, a national directory of Spiritualists listed his circle under Indiana: Cathcart's Spirit Room, Laporte.
lines.tts: By eighteen fifty-eight, a national directory of Spiritualists listed his circle under Indiana: Cathcart's Spirit Room, Laporte.
lines.lower: The Spiritualist Register | 1858

lines.say: And in 1870, in her history of American Spiritualism, the medium Emma Hardinge gave it a chapter of its own: Cathcart's Spirit Room.
lines.tts: And in eighteen seventy, in her history of American Spiritualism, the medium Emma Hardinge gave it a chapter of its own: Cathcart's Spirit Room.

lines.say: We couldn't find where the spirit rooms stood. Charles Cathcart died in 1888, on his farm near La Porte. He's buried at Pine Lake Cemetery.

lines.say: Graves from the town's old city cemetery were moved here.
Not all of them had names. A marker there stands for four hundred and ninety-nine unknown persons, moved from an older burial ground.
Accounts disagree about when it happened. One says 1871. The marker itself says 1893.
lines.tts: Accounts disagree about when it happened. One says eighteen seventy-one. The marker itself says eighteen ninety-three.

lines.say: All that digging left a story behind. When one old coffin was opened, the story goes, the woman inside was found upside down and twisted, as if she had been buried alive.
We found no record of it. Stories like it are told about old cemeteries all over the world.
Visitors tell of something else: shadows, like mist, above the stones.
Elsewhere in La Porte is Patton Cemetery, begun, by one account, in 1841.
lines.tts: Elsewhere in La Porte is Patton Cemetery, begun, by one account, in eighteen forty-one.

lines.say: Andrew Helgelien, a victim of Belle Gunness, is buried there. His stone calls him the last victim. His story is in our last documentary.
lines.lower: Andrew Helgelien's grave | on a 1908 postcard

lines.say: A neighbor once told of hearing voices in the cemetery at night, and looking out to find no one there.

This year, the trouble at Patton has been the weather. The derecho of August eleventh, 2026, brought gusts near sixty miles an hour to La Porte. Afterward, the historical society said the cemetery was unsafe for the public to enter, and canceled its October tour.

lines.say: In the farm country northeast of La Porte, in Galena Township, there's a small cemetery called Posey Chapel.
In 2011, when a local newspaper counted down the county's ten most haunted places, Posey Chapel was number one.
lines.tts: In twenty eleven, when a local newspaper counted down the county's ten most haunted places, Posey Chapel was number one.

v.cap: La Porte County's most haunted, by one 2011 count

lines.say: The legend, as it's told online: the church burned more than a hundred and fifty years ago, and its preacher took his own life near the gate.
Since then, people say, there have been lights in the trees, red eyes, a woman in white, and on some nights, the sound of a woman singing.
Here's what the records say.
A Methodist congregation was founded here in 1833, a year after the county itself.
lines.tts: A Methodist congregation was founded here in eighteen thirty-three, a year after the county itself.
lines.lower: A La Porte County farm | from the 1874 county atlas

lines.say: The county's first history, written in 1876, tells how its chapel began. A Methodist minister named Posey, sent to Galena Township, talked his congregation into building one.
lines.tts: The county's first history, written in eighteen seventy-six, tells how its chapel began. A Methodist minister named Posey, sent to Galena Township, talked his congregation into building one.
lines.lower: Jasper Packard, History of La Porte County | 1876

lines.say: Neighbors came from eight or ten miles away and worked for a week. The log chapel stood on an acre of land given by Whitman Goit, and it was named Posey Chapel, for the preacher who founded it.
By 1876, the log chapel had been torn down and replaced with a frame church. One modern writer says a fire came first, in 1855. If so, there really was a fire more than a hundred and fifty years ago.
lines.tts: By eighteen seventy-six, the log chapel had been torn down and replaced with a frame church. One modern writer says a fire came first, in eighteen fifty-five. If so, there really was a fire more than a hundred and fifty years ago.

By 1876: a frame church in its place.
One modern account: a fire in 1855.

lines.say: And there was another. In 1972, the church burned again, and this time it wasn't rebuilt. That writer says the fire was set on purpose.
lines.tts: And there was another. In nineteen seventy-two, the church burned again, and this time it wasn't rebuilt. That writer says the fire was set on purpose.

lines.say: Today, a pavilion stands where the chapel stood, among hundreds of graves.
As for the preacher, there really was one, and the chapel carries his name. But we found no record that any preacher there took his own life, and no record of anyone dying in either fire.
It's still an active cemetery, where families bury their own. If you go, go by day, and leave it as you found it.
On July thirty-first, 1905, the Muncie Evening Press ran a story about a ghost near La Porte, under the headline Headless Ghost Grows Uneasy.
lines.tts: On July thirty-first, nineteen oh five, the Muncie Evening Press ran a story about a ghost near La Porte, under the headline Headless Ghost Grows Uneasy.

lines.say: Within two weeks, versions of the story were running in newspapers as far away as Connecticut, Virginia and Kansas.
lines.lower: Barbour County Index, Medicine Lodge, Kansas | Aug. 16, 1905

lines.say: It told of a place called Flaherty's Siding, where, after dark, a figure had been seen on the railroad platform.
It had no head. It carried a dinner pail, and it swung its arms as if it were flagging an approaching train.
lines.lower: “The Headless Apparition” | a newspaper drawing, 1905

lines.say: Then it would vanish, often with a shriek.
Headless, the paper said, and acting for all the world like an animate thing.
People believed it was Columbus Cole, a well-known local man who had been run over by an engine, close to the spot where the water tank stood. The accident, the paper said, had taken his head.
lines.lower: New Haven Morning Journal and Courier | Aug. 14, 1905, from the Indianapolis Sentinel

lines.say: But in another version, printed in Kansas and Virginia, Cole had died in a boiler explosion that blew off the top of his head. Even in 1905, the story wouldn't hold still.
lines.tts: But in another version, printed in Kansas and Virginia, Cole had died in a boiler explosion that blew off the top of his head. Even in nineteen oh five, the story wouldn't hold still.
lines.lower: Barbour County Index | Aug. 16, 1905

lines.say: Some young men from town decided it was a hoax, and went out to prove it.
The first night, they saw nothing.
On the second night, one of them called for quiet. There, near the old water tank, stood the headless figure. They watched it for five minutes or more.
Then they ran to the spot. It was gone.
By one account, they recognized the dinner pail: the one Cole always carried to and from work. We were no longer skeptics, the paper quoted them, but believers.

We tried to find Columbus Cole. The Indianapolis version put the water tank on the Lake Erie railway. But we couldn't find a record of Cole's death, or even where Flaherty's Siding was. If you know, tell us in the comments.

v.head: STILL UNKNOWN

on the Lake Erie line near La Porte.

lines.say: And if you go looking, stay off the tracks. Trains still run through La Porte County, and they don't stop for ghosts.

lines.say: In the fall of 1940, before the United States entered the Second World War, the government picked farmland south of La Porte for an ammunition plant.
lines.tts: In the fall of nineteen forty, before the United States entered the Second World War, the government picked farmland south of La Porte for an ammunition plant.

v.lower: “The defense program comes to the cornfield” | a federal booklet, about 1941

lines.say: It took in more than thirteen thousand acres. About two hundred and fifty families had to leave their homes and farms.

v.lower: Rail spur and storage yard, Kingsbury | about 1941

lines.say: The Kingsbury Ordnance Plant loaded shells and assembled fuses, up to a hundred and eighty thousand fuses a day.
lines.lower: A storehouse for finished ammunition, going up | Kingsbury, about 1941

lines.say: In May 1942, it employed twenty thousand, seven hundred and eighty-five people. Nearly half of them were women.
lines.tts: In May nineteen forty-two, it employed twenty thousand, seven hundred and eighty-five people. Nearly half of them were women.

v.cap: workers, May 1942; nearly half of them women

lines.say: To house them, builders started nearly three thousand homes in a new town, laid out in a circle like a wagon wheel. At first, it was called Victory City. Today it's Kingsford Heights.
lines.lower: Kingsford Heights | U.S. Geological Survey map, 1958

lines.say: The work was dangerous. An explosive called tetryl turned some workers' skin orange.
In that 2011 list of the county's most haunted places, the plant was number ten. The writer said she'd been told that explosions had killed workers there during the war.
lines.tts: In that twenty eleven list of the county's most haunted places, the plant was number ten. The writer said she'd been told that explosions had killed workers there during the war.

lines.say: We found no record of deadly explosions there. One writer who researched the plant says there were never any major accidents.
The plant closed after the war, reopened for the Korean War, and closed for good around 1960.
lines.tts: The plant closed after the war, reopened for the Korean War, and closed for good around nineteen sixty.

lines.say: In 1965, much of the land went to the state. Today it's the Kingsbury Fish and Wildlife Area, where people hunt, fish and hike.
lines.tts: In nineteen sixty-five, much of the land went to the state. Today it's the Kingsbury Fish and Wildlife Area, where people hunt, fish and hike.
lines.lower: The old plant land, from the air | 2025

lines.say: Other parts of the old plant are private industrial land, and off-limits. If you go, stay on public land, and wear orange in hunting season.
Sometimes a place feels haunted simply because so much happened there, and so few people remember.
Most of these stories can't be proved. And the records don't back up some of them at all.

But the people in them were real. A keeper who climbed to her lamp for forty-three years. A congressman who sat in the dark and listened. Four hundred and ninety-nine people no one could name. A congregation that lost its church. A man the paper called Columbus Cole. And twenty thousand workers who went to war without going overseas.
Maybe that's what a ghost story is: a way of remembering.
The Old Lighthouse Museum is open Wednesday through Sunday afternoons until the end of October.
The cemeteries are active, and they belong to the families. Go by day, be respectful, and stay off private land.
